Data domain computation creates signatures that are more spread-out, selecting more noisy volume samples which are false positives [S2].

The claim is directly supported by the text in Source [S2]. The notes explicitly state that 'Data domain computation creates signatures that are more spread-out, selecting more noisy volume samples which are false positives.' This is corroborated by the passage which states: 'The data domain computation (Figure 13 (b)) creates signatures that are more spread-out... More noisy volume samples from the data domain computation are selected (Figure 13 (b)), and they are found to be false positives.'
supported
Spatial domain computation is more reliable and robust for data with spatial embedding, whereas data domain computation introduces more noisy volume samples (false positives) [S2].

The claim is directly supported by the text in Source [S2]. The notes explicitly state that 'Spatial domain computation is more reliable and robust for data with spatial embedding, whereas data domain computation introduces more noisy volume samples (false positives).' Furthermore, the passage confirms this by stating, 'More noisy volume samples from the data domain computation are selected... and they are found to be false positives... Therefore, the data domain variant is not robust for data with spatial embedding, whereas the spatial computation is more reliable.'
supported
These IDs are used to sort the returned partial images from processors before compositing them into the final image [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that IDs are used to sort returned partial images from processors before compositing them into the final image. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Use these IDs to sort the returned partial images from processors before compositing them into the final image' and 'For composite time ordering each partial image gets the ID corresponding to its data block.' This confirms that the evidence supports the claim.
supported
The process iterates through blocks in the $x$-direction, incrementing the ID by $1$ for each subsequent block until no more blocks exist in the current $y$-$z$ plane [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the process iterates through blocks in the x-direction, incrementing the ID by 1 for each subsequent block until no more blocks exist in the current y-z plane. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Then pick up the next block in the x direction and assign it an ID of 2. In a similar manner IDs are assigned to all the blocks in the x direction until there are no more. After that again start from x = 0 but with the next y block...'. This confirms the iteration direction (x), the incrementing nature of the ID assignment, and the stopping condition (until no more blocks exist in the current plane defined by y and z coordinates).
supported
An algorithm to assign unique integer IDs to data blocks to determine the rendering/compositing order, ensuring correct depth ordering during parallel volume rendering [S1, unofficial].

The claim accurately describes the algorithm detailed in Source [S1]. The source explicitly states that an algorithm assigns unique integer IDs to data blocks starting from (0,0,0) with ID 1, incrementing along the X, then Y, then Z axes, to determine the rendering/compositing order and ensure correct depth ordering.
supported

Two variants for computing indexed points: Spatial domain computation (filters out false positives outside spatial neighborhoods) and Data domain computation (creates more spread-out signatures) [S2].

The claim accurately reflects the information provided in Source [S2]. The source explicitly states that there are two variants: Spatial domain computation and Data domain computation. It confirms that spatial domain computation filters out false positives outside spatial neighborhoods and is more reliable/robust for data with spatial embedding. It also confirms that data domain computation creates more spread-out signatures and selects more noisy volume samples (false positives).
supported
Each partial image is assigned the ID corresponding to its source data block for composite time ordering [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that each partial image is assigned the ID corresponding to its source data block for composite time ordering. The evidence explicitly states in the bullet points: 'Assign each partial image the ID corresponding to its source data block for composite time ordering.' Additionally, the passage text confirms: 'For composite time ordering each partial image gets the ID corresponding to its data block.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
The ID assignment starts at $(0,0,0)$ with ID $1$, then increments along the $X$ axis, then $Y$, then $Z$ [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that ID assignment starts at coordinates (0,0,0) with ID 1. It further details the iteration process: incrementing along the X axis first, then moving to the next Y block (resetting X), and finally moving to the next Z block (resetting X and Y). This matches the claim exactly.
supported
Finally, it resets $x$ and $y$ to $0$, increments $z$ to the next block, and repeats the process until all blocks in the $3D$ grid have an ID [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the process resets $x$ and $y$ to 0, increments $z$ to the next block, and repeats until all blocks have an ID. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Then again start from x=0 and y=0 with the next z block and continue this processes until all blocks have an ID.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
It then resets $x$ to $0$, increments $y$ to the next block, and repeats the $x$-direction iteration until the entire $y$-dimension is covered [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the process resets x to 0, increments y to the next block, and repeats the x-direction iteration until the entire y-dimension is covered. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'After that again start from x = 0 but with the next y block and this process continues until the whole y dimension is covered.' This matches the claim exactly.
